items.title: Ford's $5 day was a retention crisis fix, not generosity
items.claim: In January 1914, Henry Ford doubled the basic wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day. What problem was he solving?

options.text: Falling demand for the Model T
Catastrophic worker turnover — the assembly line was so monotonous that annual turnover had reached around 370%, meaning the plant had to hire roughly 50,000 people to maintain a workforce of 14,000
Pressure from Theodore Roosevelt's administration
A unionisation drive he wanted to prevent

items.reveal:
Daniel Raff and Lawrence Summers's 1987 paper analysed Ford's wage decision. Turnover collapsed after the announcement; absenteeism dropped from 10% to 2.5%; productivity rose. The wage was conditional — there was a 'Sociological Department' that inspected workers' homes for 'good moral character' to qualify.

The popular story (Ford paid workers enough to buy his cars) is a post-hoc rationalisation. A Model T cost roughly $440; a workforce of 14,000 buying cars wouldn't move the market.

The wage was efficient: Ford gained productivity worth more than the extra wage bill.
items.why: Famous 'visionary' business decisions usually have boring, specific operational drivers. The $5 day looks like generosity; it was wage-efficiency arbitrage.

items.title: Market research said the Walkman would fail
items.claim: Sony launched the TPS-L2 Walkman in 1979. What did market research suggest beforehand?

options.text: Strong demand from young consumers — supporting the launch
Likely failure: consumers reported they wanted recording capability, not just playback, and disliked the absence of speakers
Research correctly predicted enormous success
No research was conducted because Akio Morita had no money for it

items.reveal:
Co-founder Masaru Ibuka wanted a portable player so he could listen to opera on long flights. Akio Morita, despite hostile focus group findings, championed the launch. Sony hedged by initially offering it with two headphone jacks (so you could share) and a 'hotline' button to talk to a companion — both later dropped.

First-month sales in Japan were 30,000 units. By the early 1980s the Walkman was a global phenomenon and 'walkman' became a generic word for portable cassette player.

Clayton Christensen later used the case in 'The Innovator's Dilemma' to argue that existing customer research can't reliably predict demand for genuinely new products.
items.why: Market research has methodological limits. Consumers can tell you what they want among options they already know; they're worse at imagining a category that doesn't exist.

items.title: Blockbuster could have bought Netflix for $50 million in 2000
items.claim: In 2000, Netflix was a struggling DVD-by-mail service. What did Blockbuster's CEO John Antioco do when Reed Hastings flew to Dallas to propose a sale?

options.text: Agreed in principle but the deal collapsed over terms
Laughed Hastings out of the room
Counter-offered to buy Netflix for $200 million
Bought a minority stake to monitor the technology

items.reveal_title: The room where it didn't happen
items.reveal:
Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph have both told the story (Randolph's book 'That Will Never Work' has the most colour). They proposed Blockbuster acquire Netflix for $50 million and run blockbuster.com as the online arm. Antioco — facing a profitable late-fee business model — declined.

Blockbuster did later launch an online service (Blockbuster Online) and was on a recovery path under Antioco, but a 2005 boardroom fight with activist investor Carl Icahn led to Antioco's departure and the strategy's reversal. Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010.

Netflix's market cap is now over $300 billion.
items.why: Disruption isn't usually about technology incumbents can't access; it's about business models they can't bring themselves to attack. Late fees were too profitable to risk.

items.title: Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975
items.claim: Steven Sasson, a Kodak engineer, built the first digital camera prototype in 1975. What happened to it?

options.text: Kodak rushed it to market and dominated the digital camera industry
Kodak management, worried about cannibalising film sales, suppressed the project; the company filed for bankruptcy in 2012 having failed the digital transition
It was stolen by a competitor before it could be developed
Sasson left and founded Nikon

items.reveal:
Sasson's prototype was a 3.6 kg device using a CCD sensor and a cassette tape, taking 23 seconds to capture a 0.01 megapixel black-and-white image. He filed a patent in 1978.

Kodak's response, as Sasson later recalled, was 'that's cute, but don't tell anyone about it.' Film and processing had 60-70% gross margins. Kodak did launch digital products from the 1990s but couldn't restructure around a business model with lower margins.

The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2012.
items.why: Owning the future technology isn't enough — you have to be willing to destroy your current revenue. Few large organisations can.

items.title: Maslow's pyramid was never drawn by Maslow
items.claim: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs is taught with a pyramid. What did Maslow himself draw?

options.text: He drew the pyramid himself in his 1943 paper
He never drew it as a pyramid; the pyramid representation was introduced by management consultants and textbooks in the 1960s
He drew it as a circle to indicate non-linear progression
He explicitly rejected any visual representation

items.reveal:
Todd Bridgman, Stephen Cummings and John Ballard's 2019 paper in the Academy of Management Learning & Education traced the pyramid to Charles McDermid's 1960 management article in Business Horizons. Maslow's 1943 'A Theory of Human Motivation' described needs as overlapping and dynamic — not rigidly tiered.

Maslow himself, late in his career, qualified the theory heavily: needs can be pursued in parallel, prioritisation varies by culture and individual, and self-actualisation isn't a 'top' level so much as a developmental orientation.

Empirical tests find weak support for the strict hierarchy.
items.why: The most-taught motivation diagram in business education was drawn by someone other than the named theorist and oversimplifies what he wrote. Worth checking what's in the textbook against what's in the source.

items.title: Accounting profit and economic profit measure different things
items.claim: A bakery reports £80,000 accounting profit. The owner could earn £50,000 in alternative employment and £15,000 by renting out the premises. What is the economic profit?
items.reveal:
Accounting profit deducts only explicit costs. Economic profit also deducts opportunity costs — the next-best foregone returns to the owner's time and assets. Here: £80,000 - £50,000 - £15,000 = £15,000.

A business with positive accounting profit but negative economic profit is destroying value relative to alternatives. The distinction was formalised by Alfred Marshall in his 'Principles of Economics' (1890).
items.why: A firm reporting profit on its income statement may still be the wrong use of the owner's resources. Accounting standards weren't designed to answer that question.

items.title: Depreciation methods change reported profit, not cash
items.claim: A delivery van costs £40,000 with a 4-year useful life and £8,000 residual value. Under straight-line depreciation, what is the year-1 depreciation charge?
items.reveal_title: Straight-line: (cost minus residual) divided by life
items.reveal:
(£40,000 - £8,000) / 4 = £8,000 per year. Reducing balance would front-load the charge (e.g. 40% of £40,000 = £16,000 in year 1).

Neither method affects cash flow — the van was paid for upfront. Depreciation is an accounting allocation that matches cost to revenue across periods, governed by IAS 16. Different methods produce different reported profits in early years but the same total over the asset's life.
items.why: Profit figures are sensitive to accounting policy choices. Cash flow is not. This is one reason cash flow statements were made mandatory under IAS 7.

items.title: Quick ratio strips out the inventory you can't sell fast
items.claim: A retailer has current assets of £600,000 (including £400,000 inventory) and current liabilities of £300,000. What is the quick (acid-test) ratio?
items.reveal:
Quick ratio = (current assets - inventory) / current liabilities = (£600,000 - £400,000) / £300,000 = 0.67. Current ratio would be 2.0 — looking healthy. The acid-test reveals the firm could not cover short-term liabilities without selling stock.

The rule of thumb that quick ratio should exceed 1.0 is industry-dependent. Supermarkets routinely operate below 0.5 because they sell stock for cash before paying suppliers.
items.why: Two firms with identical current ratios can have very different real liquidity. Inventory turnover matters as much as the ratio number.

items.title: ROCE compares like with like across firm sizes
items.claim: A firm has operating profit of £2 million, total assets of £15 million and current liabilities of £5 million. What is ROCE?
items.reveal_title: Operating profit divided by capital employed
items.reveal:
Capital employed = total assets - current liabilities = £15m - £5m = £10m. ROCE = £2m / £10m = 20%.

ROCE is the most commonly cited single profitability measure in UK A-level. It is benchmarked against the cost of capital — if a firm consistently earns less than its weighted cost of capital, it is destroying shareholder value. UK FTSE 100 firms have averaged 10-15% ROCE over the last decade.
items.why: Absolute profit figures don't tell you whether capital was well used. A £2m profit from £10m of capital is 20%; the same profit from £100m of capital is 2%.

items.title: High gearing is risk, not failure
items.claim: A firm has long-term debt of £40 million and equity of £60 million. Its gearing ratio (debt / debt+equity) is 40%. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Gearing this high is always dangerous
Higher gearing magnifies returns to shareholders in good times and losses in bad — utilities routinely run 60%+ because cash flows are stable
Gearing measures liquidity
Equity is always cheaper than debt

items.reveal:
UK water and electricity utilities (Severn Trent, National Grid) often carry gearing above 60% because regulated cash flows make debt servicing predictable. Tech firms (pre-2022) often had near-zero gearing because cash flows were volatile and equity was cheap.

Modigliani and Miller (1958) argued that, in perfect markets, capital structure is irrelevant. In real markets — with taxes, bankruptcy costs and asymmetric information — there is an optimal range. Lehman Brothers' gearing reached above 30:1 (debt:equity) before its 2008 collapse.
items.why: Whether high gearing is reckless depends on what cash flows look like. The number alone tells you little.

items.title: Profitable businesses fail when cash runs out
items.claim: A construction firm books £5 million revenue and £500,000 profit in 2023 but customers pay 120 days after invoicing while suppliers demand 30 days. What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: Strong cash position because of the reported profit
A cash flow gap large enough to threaten survival, despite profitability — overtrading
Profit and cash will be identical
Suppliers must accept 120-day payment by law

items.reveal:
Carillion, the UK construction giant, reported £147 million profit in 2016 and collapsed in January 2018 with £1.5 billion of debt. A large part of the gap between profit and cash came from long receivable cycles on government contracts combined with aggressive revenue recognition.

'Profit is opinion; cash is fact' is an accounting saying with an empirical basis. The UK Insolvency Service reports that 80%+ of business failures involve a cash-flow rather than profitability problem.
items.why: Reported profit can lead, lag or diverge from cash entirely. Working capital management is often what separates surviving and failing firms.

items.title: Break-even with multiple products needs a sales mix
items.claim: A bakery sells two products. Bread has £2 contribution per unit; cakes have £5. Fixed costs are £14,000. Without knowing the sales mix, what can you calculate?

options.text: A single break-even quantity
You cannot calculate one break-even point — only break-even combinations or a break-even assuming a fixed sales mix ratio
Break-even is always the average contribution divided into fixed costs
You need the selling price as well

items.reveal:
If the bakery historically sells 3 loaves per cake, weighted contribution per 'bundle' = 3 x £2 + 1 x £5 = £11. Break-even = £14,000 / £11 = 1,273 bundles = 3,820 loaves + 1,273 cakes.

Change the mix and the break-even quantity changes. This is why textbook single-product break-even questions are misleading guides to multi-product reality. Real firms use 'weighted contribution' or 'break-even sales value' instead.
items.why: The simple Y = a + bX break-even chart assumes one product. Few real firms have only one product, which is why management accounting moves to contribution margin analysis.

items.title: Just-in-time becomes a vulnerability under shock
items.claim: Toyota pioneered just-in-time inventory. What happened to Toyota production during the 2011 Tohoku earthquake?

options.text: JIT prevented any disruption
Toyota's global production fell by around 800,000 vehicles because a single supplier of microcontrollers (Renesas) was damaged
Toyota switched to mass-production overnight
Toyota had no Japanese suppliers

items.reveal:
Renesas's Naka factory in Ibaraki produced ~30% of automotive microcontrollers globally. After the 11 March 2011 earthquake, Toyota's worldwide output dropped sharply through to mid-2011. After Tohoku, Toyota mandated suppliers to map upstream dependencies and hold buffer stocks for critical components — partially abandoning pure JIT.

The 2020-22 COVID semiconductor shortages repeated the lesson industry-wide.
items.why: Lean optimises against ordinary variation. It does not optimise against catastrophic disruption — and the same firms that pioneered it have had to add 'just-in-case' buffers.

items.title: Maximising capacity utilisation isn't always optimal
items.claim: A factory runs at 95% capacity utilisation. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: This is always the optimal level
Running close to maximum capacity leaves no slack for demand surges, breakdowns or staff absence and tends to raise unit costs through overtime and quality problems
Capacity utilisation has no link to unit cost
Unit costs fall continuously with utilisation

items.reveal:
Hospitals running at >90% bed occupancy have measurably worse patient outcomes (NHS England analyses through the 2010s). Airlines running above 85% load factor face cascading delay risk. Manufacturing plants above 90% have higher defect rates and overtime costs.

Operations researchers use Kingman's formula: waiting time grows non-linearly as utilisation approaches 100%. The textbook assumption that high utilisation is good ignores queueing dynamics.
items.why: Headline utilisation numbers hide trade-offs. The optimal level depends on demand variability, not just on fixed-cost recovery.

items.title: Quality assurance and quality control are different things
items.claim: A car plant inspects every vehicle at the end of the line and rejects defective units. Which approach is this?

options.text: Quality assurance, because it ensures quality
Quality control — defect detection after the fact. Quality assurance builds quality into the process so defects don't arise
Total Quality Management
ISO 9001 certification

items.reveal:
W. Edwards Deming, who worked in postwar Japan, argued that inspecting defects out is more expensive than preventing them. His '14 Points' for management (1986) included 'cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality'.

Toyota's andon-cord system stops the line whenever a worker sees a problem — quality is built upstream. Quality control still happens, but as a back-stop, not the main mechanism. ISO 9001 audits processes (assurance), not products (control).
items.why: Two firms with identical defect rates can have very different cost structures depending on whether defects are prevented or caught.

items.title: COVID exposed how thin most supply chains were
items.claim: During 2020-22, automotive production was held back by shortages of one component category in particular. Which was it?

options.text: Aluminium
Semiconductors (chips) — the global shortage cost the automotive industry an estimated $210 billion in lost revenue in 2021 alone (AlixPartners)
Rubber tyres
Steel

items.reveal:
When auto demand fell in spring 2020, car makers cancelled chip orders. Foundries (TSMC, Samsung) reallocated capacity to consumer electronics, where demand was surging. When car demand returned, chip capacity was booked out. Ford alone lost around 1.25 million units of production in 2021.

The US CHIPS Act (2022) and EU Chips Act (2023) responded with $50bn+ in subsidies for domestic semiconductor manufacturing — a direct strategic response to the disruption.
items.why: Multi-tier supply chains hide concentration risk. A car maker can have hundreds of direct suppliers but still depend on two or three foundries for chips.

items.title: Herzberg's hygiene factors don't motivate
items.claim: Frederick Herzberg's 1959 'Motivation to Work' surveyed 200 engineers and accountants. What did he conclude about pay?

options.text: Pay was the strongest motivator
Pay is a 'hygiene factor' — low pay causes dissatisfaction but high pay does not produce sustained motivation. Motivators are achievement, recognition and the work itself
Pay had no effect either way
Only senior staff are motivated by pay

items.reveal:
Herzberg's two-factor theory splits job factors into hygiene (pay, conditions, supervision, policies) — whose absence causes dissatisfaction — and motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth) — which actively drive engagement.

Methodological critics note Herzberg used the 'critical incident' interview technique, in which people tend to attribute good experiences to themselves and bad ones to external factors. Replications using other methods get less crisp results.
items.why: Pay rises buy off dissatisfaction, not loyalty or effort. Most modern HR practice combines compensation (hygiene) with job design (motivators) — a direct legacy of Herzberg.

items.title: Taylor's piece rate was an incentive, not a wage
items.claim: F.W. Taylor at Bethlehem Steel in the 1890s introduced piece-rate pay. What was the central design feature?

options.text: All workers received the same base pay regardless of output
Workers were paid per unit produced, with the 'scientific' target set so only those following Taylor's prescribed method could earn the bonus
Piece rates were determined by union negotiation
Workers shared profits collectively

items.reveal_title: Pay per piece, conditional on method
items.reveal:
Taylor's pig-iron handling experiments at Bethlehem Steel (1898-99) raised loading from 12.5 to 47 tons per worker per day. Workers earning the bonus received about 60% more pay; the firm got 280% more output per worker.

Unions opposed Taylorism fiercely — 1911 US Congressional hearings investigated 'speed-up' abuses. Modern piece rates persist in garment factories, gig economy (Uber surge pricing as a variant) and sales commissions.
items.why: Piece rates align effort with output but can erode quality, safety and worker autonomy. The same design principle reappears in 'pay for performance' compensation a century later.

items.title: The Hawthorne effect is real but smaller than the textbook story
items.claim: Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies (1927-32) are taught as showing that worker productivity rose because of attention paid to them. What does re-analysis of the original data show?

options.text: The effect was even larger than originally reported

Levitt and List's 2011 re-analysis of original records suggests the 'Hawthorne effect' was much weaker than reported; productivity gains were largely explained by which workers were replaced and the Monday rebound after weekends
No data from the studies survived
The lighting reduction was actually the cause

items.reveal:
Steven Levitt and John List (American Economic Journal, 2011) accessed original Hawthorne Works data digitised by the University of Wisconsin. They found the famous 'productivity rose whatever you changed' pattern was much weaker than Mayo claimed and largely artifactual.

The broader 'human relations' school it spawned remained influential — but the founding evidence base was weaker than generations of textbooks suggested.
items.why: Iconic findings get retold long after the evidence has been challenged. Modern HR theory survives, but its founding study should be taught with caveats.

items.title: UK Supreme Court ruled Uber drivers were workers, not self-employed
items.claim: In February 2021, the UK Supreme Court ruled on the employment status of Uber drivers. What did it decide?

options.text: Drivers were correctly classified as self-employed
Drivers were 'workers' under UK law, entitled to minimum wage, paid holiday and pension auto-enrolment
Drivers were 'employees' with full unfair-dismissal rights
Uber was banned from operating in the UK

items.reveal:
The case ran from a 2016 Employment Tribunal decision to the Supreme Court. Lord Leggatt's judgment held that Uber's contract terms could not displace the reality of control: Uber set fares, terms, the rating system and routes.

Uber subsequently announced UK drivers would be paid minimum wage and pension contributions. The judgment did not give drivers full 'employee' status (no protection against unfair dismissal). Similar litigation has run in California, France and the Netherlands.
items.why: UK employment law has three statuses (employee, worker, self-employed). The 'worker' middle category was created in 1996; gig economy litigation has been the main test of where the line falls.

items.title: The 7Ps were extended for services, not because the 4Ps were wrong
items.claim: The original 4Ps (product, price, place, promotion) were proposed by E. Jerome McCarthy in 1960. Why were three more Ps added later?

options.text: Because McCarthy retracted his framework
Booms and Bitner (1981) added people, process and physical evidence to capture the special characteristics of service industries (intangibility, inseparability, variability, perishability)
Because competition law required disclosure
Because digital marketing required four extra Ps

items.reveal:
Bernard Booms and Mary Bitner's 1981 chapter 'Marketing Strategies and Organization Structures for Service Firms' added People (staff interactions with customers), Process (service delivery procedures) and Physical evidence (the tangible elements customers see).

A haircut, a flight or a consultation can't be inventoried, tested or returned. The 4Ps work better for tangible goods than for services, which by 2020 made up around 80% of UK GDP.
items.why: Frameworks evolve as the economy does. The 7Ps reflect a shift toward services that has continued since 1981.

items.title: Decline is not the end — vinyl records came back
items.claim: Vinyl record sales collapsed from the mid-1980s as CDs took over. What has happened since the late 2000s?

options.text: Vinyl remained obsolete
Vinyl sales have risen every year from 2007 to 2023, overtaking CDs in US revenue terms in 2022 for the first time since 1987 (RIAA data)
Vinyl was banned in 2010
CDs grew alongside vinyl

items.reveal:
RIAA US data: vinyl revenue fell to under $20m by 2006. By 2022, vinyl revenue was $1.2bn — overtaking CDs ($483m) for the first time in 35 years. UK Official Charts data shows similar pattern from 2008 onwards.

The textbook PLC implies decline is terminal. Brand repositioning, nostalgia and physical-product premiums in a streaming world reversed that trajectory. Other examples: Polaroid film, Kodak Super 8, mechanical watches.
items.why: The four-stage product life cycle is a framework, not a law of nature. Decline can be reversed by changing what the product means to customers.

items.title: Ansoff said diversification was the riskiest growth strategy
items.claim: Igor Ansoff's 1957 'Strategies for Diversification' in Harvard Business Review introduced a 2x2 matrix. Which growth strategy did he flag as carrying highest risk?

options.text: Market penetration
Diversification (new product, new market) — combining product and market uncertainty multiplies risk
Product development
Market development

items.reveal:
Ansoff's matrix sequences risk: market penetration (existing product, existing market) is safest; product development and market development each add one source of uncertainty; diversification adds two.

Empirical work (Markides 1995, McKinsey 2010s) has supported this in aggregate: unrelated diversification destroys shareholder value more often than not. The 1960s conglomerate boom (ITT, Hanson) and its 1990s breakup vindicated Ansoff's warning.
items.why: Growth strategies look attractive on the upside; Ansoff's matrix forces you to articulate the downside risks for each route.

items.title: Demographics often predict less than marketers assume
items.claim: Mark Ritson and others have argued that traditional demographic segmentation (age, income, gender) often performs poorly. What's the evidence?

options.text: Demographics predict purchase behaviour with high accuracy
Within-group variation in purchase behaviour is often larger than between-group variation; behavioural segmentation (what people actually buy) typically outperforms demographic segmentation
Demographics are legally required for marketing
Segmentation has been abandoned in modern marketing

items.reveal:
Byron Sharp's 'How Brands Grow' (2010), drawing on the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, argued that mass-market brands grow through reach, not narrow targeting — and that demographic targeting often misallocates spend. Coca-Cola buyers, Toyota buyers and HSBC customers look broadly similar demographically.

Behavioural segmentation (heavy vs light buyers, lapsed vs active) typically explains more variance. Geographic and psychographic add incremental power.
items.why: Marketing teaching often defaults to demographic segmentation because it's easy to teach and the data is available. The evidence suggests it's a weaker guide than is taught.

items.title: Brand value can exceed half of market capitalisation
items.claim: Interbrand's 2023 Best Global Brands ranking valued Apple's brand at around $502 billion. What's the relationship between brand value and accounting?

options.text: Brand value appears directly on the balance sheet for all firms
Under IFRS / UK GAAP, internally generated brands are not recognised as balance sheet assets; purchased brands can be. Apple's $502bn estimate is an external valuation, not a reported figure
Brand value equals market cap minus debt
Brand value has no relationship with share price

items.reveal:
IAS 38 prohibits capitalising internally generated brands; accounting wants to avoid the manipulability of self-assessed intangibles. Acquired brands (e.g. Cadbury bought by Kraft for £11.5bn in 2010) appear at acquisition cost as 'goodwill' or identified intangibles.

Interbrand, Kantar BrandZ and Brand Finance use different methodologies — discounted cash flow from brand-attributable earnings — and produce different rankings. The numbers are estimates, but the underlying point is real: a meaningful share of S&P 500 market value sits in intangibles invisible on balance sheets.
items.why: Investors price intangibles even when accountants don't book them. The gap between book and market value for brand-heavy firms is largely brand and goodwill.

items.title: Porter's framework asks about industry structure, not firms
items.claim: Michael Porter's 1979 HBR article introduced the five forces framework. What does it analyse?

options.text: A firm's internal strengths
The structural attractiveness of an industry: rivalry, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes
A firm's marketing mix
A firm's financial ratios

items.reveal:
Porter's 'How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy' (HBR, March 1979) made a structural argument: average industry profitability is set by the strength of the five forces. Some industries (pharma, software platforms) are persistently profitable; others (airlines, supermarkets) persistently low-margin.

McGahan and Porter (1997) found industry effects explained 19% of business unit profitability variance — less than firm effects (32%) but real. Critics (including Henry Mintzberg) argue the framework underweights innovation, complementors and network effects, which 1979 industry economics didn't see clearly.
items.why: Strategy starts with which industry you're competing in, not how cleverly you compete. Some industries make it nearly impossible to earn supernormal returns.

items.title: PESTLE is a checklist, not a model
items.claim: PESTLE analysis covers Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal and Environmental factors. What is its main analytical limitation?

options.text: It can predict the future with high accuracy
It generates an inventory of factors but does not weight them, link them or model their interactions — students often produce long unprioritised lists
It is legally required for UK firms
It only applies to large firms

items.reveal_title: A scanning tool, not a strategy
items.reveal:
PESTLE (originally PEST, expanded over time) traces to Francis Aguilar's 'Scanning the Business Environment' (1967). It's a structured way to spot environmental change but provides no mechanism to prioritise or combine factors.

Scenario planning (Royal Dutch Shell, from Pierre Wack in the 1970s) goes further: it builds plausible coherent futures and tests strategy against them. PESTLE feeds into scenario planning, not the other way around.
items.why: PESTLE is useful for ensuring you haven't missed an external factor. It's not a strategy tool on its own.

items.title: SWOT analysis is often misused as a sorting exercise
items.claim: SWOT analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) emerged from Albert Humphrey's work at Stanford in the 1960s-70s. What's the standard critique?

options.text: It is a complete strategic plan
SWOT identifies factors but provides no method to translate them into strategy; without TOWS-style cross-pairing (S-O, S-T, W-O, W-T), it's just four bullet-point lists
It can only be used for new ventures
Strengths and weaknesses cannot overlap

items.reveal:
Heinz Weihrich's 1982 TOWS matrix paired Strengths with Opportunities (offensive strategies), Strengths with Threats (defensive), Weaknesses with Opportunities (improvement), and Weaknesses with Threats (mitigation).

The core SWOT critique is that without this step, the framework lists factors without forcing a strategic choice. Most student SWOTs stop at the list stage — which is descriptive, not strategic.
items.why: SWOT looks like analysis but often delivers sorting. The strategic value is in the combinations across quadrants.

items.title: First-mover advantage is more often a myth than a rule
items.claim: Gerard Tellis and Peter Golder studied first movers across 50 product categories. What did they find?

options.text: First movers won permanently in nearly all categories
About 47% of first movers failed and the average market share of survivors was around 10%; long-term winners were more often early followers than pioneers
First movers always lost
The data was inconclusive

items.reveal:
Tellis and Golder's 'Will and Vision' (2002) and earlier paper analysed product categories from photocopiers to disposable nappies. Pioneers identified: Chux nappies (replaced by Pampers); WordStar (overtaken by Word); Friendster and MySpace (overtaken by Facebook); AltaVista (overtaken by Google).

Later entrants benefit from market education done by pioneers, technology improvements, and clearer customer preferences. The 'first mover advantage' framing oversells a narrow set of cases (network-effect platforms) as if it were general.
items.why: Business teaching often treats first-mover advantage as a strategic prize. Empirical work suggests being the right mover at the right time is more important than being first.

items.title: CSR and financial performance — the evidence is mixed but tilts positive
items.claim: Friede, Busch and Bassen's 2015 meta-analysis aggregated over 2,000 studies on the link between ESG (environmental, social, governance) factors and corporate financial performance. What did it find?

options.text: ESG and financial performance are negatively related across the board
Around 90% of studies found a non-negative relationship; the majority showed positive correlation between ESG performance and financial performance, though magnitudes are modest
No study has examined this question
ESG is required to be at least cost-neutral by law

items.reveal:
Friede, Busch and Bassen (Journal of Sustainable Finance and Investment, 2015) reviewed 2,200 empirical studies dating back to the 1970s. About 90% reported non-negative ESG-CFP relationships; ~63% reported positive.

Milton Friedman's 1970 New York Times Magazine essay ('The Social Responsibility of Business is to Increase its Profits') argued the opposite. The empirical question turns out to be less stark than either side claims — the effect is usually positive but small, and depends on which ESG element and which industry.
items.why: Strategy debates about CSR are often conducted without reference to the evidence. The aggregate finding is messier than either 'CSR is profitable' or 'CSR is a cost' implies.

items.title: Most mergers and acquisitions destroy shareholder value
items.claim: Multiple long-run studies of M&A outcomes (KPMG, Bain, Harvard Business Review reviews) report what share of deals fail to create value for the acquiring firm's shareholders?

options.text: About 10%
About 70-90%
Exactly 50%

items.reveal:
KPMG's recurring M&A studies, Bain & Company's analyses, and Roger Martin's 2016 HBR piece 'M&A: The One Thing You Need to Get Right' all converge: 70-90% of acquisitions fail to deliver the anticipated synergies, often because the acquirer overpays.

Specific failures: AOL-Time Warner (2000, $165bn), Daimler-Chrysler (1998), Quaker-Snapple (1994), Microsoft-Nokia (2014). The 'winner's curse' (Thaler, 1988) explains why competitive bidding tends to produce winners who overestimated.

Organic growth tends to deliver more predictable returns but at a slower pace.
items.why: M&A is one of the most-used growth strategies and one of the worst-performing. The gap between expected and actual synergies is systematically positive.

items.title: Share price and intrinsic value can diverge for years
items.claim: Robert Shiller's work (Nobel 2013) showed stock prices vary much more than fundamental dividends would justify. What's the implication for share price as a measure of company performance?

options.text: Share price always equals intrinsic value at all times
Share prices can diverge from intrinsic value for extended periods (excess volatility); managers focused on quarterly share prices may make worse long-term decisions
Share price has no link to fundamentals ever
Only private firms have intrinsic value

items.reveal_title: Markets price emotions as well as cash flows
items.reveal:
Shiller's 1981 American Economic Review paper showed S&P 500 prices fluctuated 5-13x more than dividend-based fair value would justify. Tech bubble peaks (2000, 2021) and crisis troughs (2009, 2020) bookend this excess volatility.

Warren Buffett quotes Benjamin Graham: 'In the short run the market is a voting machine, in the long run a weighing machine.' Managers paid largely in stock options can be incentivised to manage the voting machine rather than build long-term weight.
items.why: Headline share price moves often reflect investor sentiment as much as company performance. Compensation and strategy that anchor on share price import this volatility.

items.title: Small business survival rates are lower than commonly thought
items.claim: ONS UK Business Demography statistics consistently show what 5-year survival rate for new UK businesses?

options.text: About 90%
Around 40% — roughly six in ten new UK businesses don't survive five years
Around 75%
Around 5%

items.reveal_title: Most new businesses don't make it
items.reveal:
ONS Business Demography data: of UK enterprises born in 2017, 39.6% survived to 2022. Year-1 survival is around 90%; the attrition is concentrated in years 2-5. SME failure causes (UK Federation of Small Businesses surveys) cluster around cash flow, late payment, and lack of management capacity.

Entrepreneurship narratives in business teaching focus on success stories. The base rate is more sobering and is one reason support programmes (start-up loans, mentoring) emphasise survival skills over growth.
items.why: Survivor bias in business case studies hides the failure rate. A textbook with only successful firms gives a misleading picture of what running a business actually involves.

items.title: Patagonia's owner gave the company to the planet
items.claim: In September 2022, Yvon Chouinard announced he was transferring ownership of Patagonia. What was the structure?

options.text: An IPO on the New York Stock Exchange
All voting stock to the Patagonia Purpose Trust (climate-aligned governance); all non-voting stock (98%) to the Holdfast Collective, with future profits funding environmental causes
A sale to a private equity buyer
A management buyout

items.reveal:
Chouinard, his wife Malinda and their two children transferred Patagonia (valued around $3bn) using two vehicles: the Purpose Trust holds voting control to ensure mission alignment; the Holdfast Collective (a 501(c)(4) nonprofit) holds economic ownership and receives roughly $100m of annual profits to fund environmental work.

The structure required the family to pay $17.5m in gift tax. The company is a B Corp (certified since 2011) — the legal structure goes much further than B Corp certification alone.

B Lab's B Corp movement, launched in 2006, certifies firms meeting social and environmental performance standards.
items.why: Corporate ownership structures shape objectives. A trust-owned firm doesn't have to maximise shareholder returns — because its 'shareholders' are not the same as a public company's.
